title: Bay Area Real Estate News: Fremont, Redwood City Housing and Alameda County Tax Bills
summary: Fremont starts six projects with 918 affordable homes, Redwood City's ELCO Yards breaks ground on 501 apartments, and Alameda County tax bills arrive.
html:
This week brought two big housing groundbreakings on either side of the Bay: Fremont is starting six affordable housing developments, and construction is now underway on 501 apartments at ELCO Yards in downtown Redwood City. Meanwhile, Alameda County property owners should be getting their 2026-2027 secured property tax bills, and the first installment comes due November 1.

Fremont Breaks Ground on Six Projects With 918 Affordable Homes

The City of Fremont says six housing developments are breaking ground this fall in Centerville, Irvington, Warm Springs and Downtown. Together they will add 918 homes for low-income households. The six projects are Arbor View, Canvas Apartments, Capital at City Center, Centerville Plaza Apartments, Fremont Warm Springs and Thornton & Post. According to the city, the rentals will serve households earning between 20% and 80% of area median income. The city has helped fund four of the six.

The city says more than 560 affordable units opened in Fremont in 2025, ranking it second in Alameda County for affordable homes completed last year. Mayor Raj Salwan said the city has cut its post-entitlement permit review to half the time the state requires. Fremont's Housing Element calls for more than 7,000 affordable units by 2031.

Capital at City Center, 3440 Walnut Avenue

This downtown project mixes for-sale and affordable rental homes. The city's upcoming-units list shows 119 affordable rental apartments at 3440 Walnut Avenue, sponsored by Pacific West Communities, with leasing expected to start in spring 2028. On the same site, Brookfield Residential is marketing 216 townhomes. Brookfield says they will range from about 1,283 to 2,096 square feet, with up to four bedrooms and three baths. Brookfield hasn't published prices yet.

Canvas, 39340 Fremont Boulevard

Also downtown, Community Development Partners has begun building Canvas, a five-story, 92-unit affordable community on a 0.72-acre lot across from the Fremont Hub, according to The Registry and Tri-City Voice. The roughly $59 million project will offer studios through three-bedroom apartments for households earning 30% to 70% of area median income. Fifteen homes are set aside for households that include a person with an intellectual or developmental disability. Completion is expected in March 2028.

What it means for you: If you're a buyer interested in new construction in central Fremont, keep an eye on the Brookfield townhomes as pricing comes out. Renters who may qualify for the affordable units can sign up for the city's Affordable Housing Interest Lists to hear when applications open. If you live near Walnut Avenue or Fremont Boulevard, expect construction activity there over the next couple of years.

Redwood City: 501 Apartments Break Ground at ELCO Yards

High Street Residential, the residential arm of Trammell Crow Company, and its partner Barings have started building two apartment buildings at ELCO Yards. ELCO Yards is a six-block mixed-use district in downtown Redwood City. According to the developer, both buildings are scheduled to open in 2029:

  • 1555 El Camino Real: 252 apartments averaging about 751 square feet, plus 5,277 square feet of ground-floor retail.
  • 113 Beech Street: 249 apartments averaging about 787 square feet.

Both buildings will have studios through three-bedroom units, and some units in each building will be affordable. REBusinessOnline reports that WRNS Studio designed the buildings and SBI Builders is the general contractor. Trammell Crow says the office and life sciences portion of ELCO Yards, led by IQHQ, is already finished and 50% leased.

The groundbreaking follows changes the Redwood City Council approved in November 2025. According to the San Mateo Daily Journal, the council let the project reserve fewer deed-restricted affordable units in exchange for a $5.8 million affordable housing impact fee paid to the city. Redwood City Pulse reports the developer said the changes were needed to make construction financially feasible. The final affordable unit count wasn't in the sources we reviewed.

What it means for you: For downtown Redwood City, this is a substantial amount of new rental housing arriving in 2029. Small landlords on the Peninsula may want to keep it in mind when planning for the coming years.

Alameda County Property Tax Bills: First Installment Due November 1

Alameda County Treasurer and Tax Collector Henry C. Levy's office is mailing more than 447,000 secured property tax bills for fiscal year 2026-2027 this month, totaling about $6.4 billion, the Alameda Post reports. Key dates:

  • First installment: due November 1, 2026, and delinquent after 5 p.m. on Thursday, December 10, 2026. Late payments get a 10% penalty.
  • Second installment: due February 1, 2027, and delinquent after 5 p.m. on Monday, April 12, 2027. Late payments get a 10% penalty plus a $10 cost.

Mailed payments go to the Treasurer and Tax Collector at PO Box 45862, San Francisco, CA 94145-0862. The county's FAQ says you can order a duplicate bill online, at the office or by calling (510) 272-6800.

What it means for you: If your lender pays your taxes through escrow, it's still worth checking that the payment goes through. If you recently bought a home, keep in mind that the county may also send a separate supplemental tax bill after a change in ownership. If you have questions about your assessment or bill, a tax professional can help.

title: Construction Begins on 501 Apartments at Redwood City's ELCO Yards
summary: Two apartment buildings with 501 homes broke ground at ELCO Yards in downtown Redwood City. Completion is targeted for 2029.
html:
The last big piece of the ELCO Yards redevelopment in downtown Redwood City is now under construction. According to an October 15, 2026 announcement from Trammell Crow Company, its residential arm, High Street Residential (HSR), and its joint venture partner Barings have broken ground on two apartment buildings. Together the buildings will hold 501 homes, and both are scheduled for completion in 2029.

This is one of the largest housing projects on the Peninsula right now. Below we cover what is being built, how the project has changed over the years, and what it may mean for people who own, rent or plan to buy near downtown Redwood City.

Where the new buildings are and what they include

According to the developer, the project is split between two addresses inside the ELCO Yards district:

  • 1555 El Camino Real: 252 apartments averaging about 751 square feet, plus 5,277 square feet of ground-floor retail.
  • 113 Beech Street: 249 apartments averaging about 787 square feet.

HSR says both buildings will offer studios through three-bedroom units, and some homes in each building will be set aside as affordable housing. The developer has not said how many. Planned amenities include rooftop decks and lounges, clubrooms, pools and spas, covered parking and coworking space. WRNS Studio, which also designed the completed commercial phase, designed both buildings. SBI Builders is the general contractor, according to REBusinessOnline.

On height, Redwood City Pulse reported that changes approved in November 2025 allowed one residential parcel, identified as Parcel A, to rise to seven stories within an 85-foot height limit. We could not confirm which of the two addresses matches Parcel A, or how tall the second building will be.

The bigger ELCO Yards picture

ELCO Yards was formerly called the South Main Mixed-Use project. It covers six blocks of downtown Redwood City, and Redwood City Pulse lists its address as 1601 El Camino Real. The city first approved the project in 2020, and work on the commercial buildings started in 2022, the Pulse reported.

According to Trammell Crow Company, the office and life sciences portion has been delivered and is about half leased. IQHQ led that portion. Reported tenants include the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, with about 224,000 square feet, and the law firm Orrick, with about 65,000 square feet. The full district is planned to include more than 600,000 square feet of office and lab space, along with childcare, restaurants, parks, plazas and public art. In its announcement, Barings pointed to the site's closeness to the Redwood City Caltrain station as a key reason for investing.

One detail doesn't line up across sources. The developer and REBusinessOnline describe ELCO Yards as having 501 apartments when finished. Earlier reporting by Redwood City Pulse on the city's approvals described 540 residential units, with nearly 150 of them affordable. We could not confirm from the sources we reviewed how those two figures fit together.

Affordable housing changes approved in 2025

Construction follows revisions that the Redwood City City Council approved in November 2025, according to Redwood City Pulse. The developer told the council that rising interest rates, inflation and other cost pressures made it hard to build a project designed before 2020 without changes. The Pulse reported that the approved changes:

  • Reduced the number of extremely low-, very low- and low-income units by 36 and increased market-rate units.
  • Added a housing impact fee of $5,822,001, where there had been no fee before.
  • Gave Redwood City residents, former residents and local workers preference for the units.
  • Made cost-saving design changes to materials such as panels, railings and windows.

The Pulse also reported that council members raised concerns about who will manage the buildings. At the time, several large property management firms were being considered.

What this may mean for Bay Area homeowners, buyers and renters

Nearby residents along El Camino Real and Beech Street, and in the blocks around downtown, can expect construction activity for the next few years. The City of Redwood City's Community Development Department is the place to go for construction notices and project documents.

Renters, including people interested in the affordable units, won't be able to apply until the buildings get close to opening in 2029. Since the units give preference to local residents and workers, it's worth watching for announcements from the city and the property manager about how and when to apply.

Small landlords who own rentals near downtown Redwood City should know that about 500 new apartments are scheduled to open around 2029. That much new supply near Caltrain could affect rent competition nearby. If you're thinking about pricing or refinancing a rental, a lender or tax professional can help you plan.

Buyers and sellers may find it helpful to follow how ELCO Yards fills in. The office space, the childcare facility and the apartments will all add activity to the area south of downtown. We'll keep tracking this project and other Peninsula and South Bay developments as they move forward.

title: San Mateo-Foster City Schools Ask Voters to Approve $498M Measure W Bond on Nov. 3
summary: Measure W would let the San Mateo-Foster City School District issue $498M in bonds at about $29 per $100,000 of assessed value. Here's what it would fund.
html:
Property owners in San Mateo and Foster City will see a school bond on the November 3, 2026 ballot. Measure W would allow the San Mateo-Foster City School District to issue up to $498 million in bonds. The district serves students from preschool through eighth grade. According to the district, the main uses would be replacing windowless and outdated classrooms, building new science, music and career-technical spaces, and creating workforce housing for teachers and staff.

Here is what the measure does, what it would cost property owners, and what buyers and sellers may want to keep in mind.

What Measure W would authorize

According to the ballot question published by Local News Matters, Measure W would authorize $498,000,000 in bonds at a levy of $29 per $100,000 of assessed value. That would raise an average of about $35 million a year while the bonds are outstanding. Patch's voter guide reports that the district expects bond payments could continue through fiscal year 2054-55. The money could not be used for regular operating costs or salaries. Like most California school facility bonds, Measure W needs 55% of the vote to pass.

The district's bond information page says the Board of Trustees ordered the election through Resolution No. 06/25-26. Under state law, oversight would include an independent citizens' oversight committee and annual audits.

Which schools and projects are on the list

The district's bond page lists these priority projects:

  • Career-technical, science and music space at Abbott Middle School
  • Replacing "pod" buildings at Audubon and San Mateo Park
  • A new science, music and library building at Bayside, and a science, music, library and administration building at Borel
  • Rebuilding the Bowditch campus
  • Districtwide work on fire alarms, roofing, windows, painting, furniture, classroom technology and libraries
  • Workforce housing

The district's estimated priority budget includes:

  • Workforce housing: $100 million
  • Replacing windowless classrooms: $84 million
  • Science, music and career-technical education: $69 million
  • Bowditch campus rebuild: $59 million
  • Classroom and site modernizations: $49 million
  • Furniture: $38 million
  • Painting: $31 million

These figures come from the district's Facilities Master Plan. The San Mateo Daily Journal reported that the board approved the plan on January 22, 2026. The plan found nearly $1.1 billion in total needs across 21 school campuses, a preschool center, a closed school and three administrative sites. At the time, Amy Ruffo, the district's executive director of Facilities and Construction, told the paper the plan lined up with priorities like windowless classrooms but was "not yet an implementation plan." We did not find a published construction schedule for individual campuses.

Bowditch Middle School in Foster City is already partly rebuilt. The Daily Journal reported that a new gym, classrooms and library opened there in May 2026, funded by the earlier bond. The master plan calls for a next phase that would demolish about two-thirds of the original buildings to make room for a turf field and outdoor courts.

The workforce housing piece

The district says part of the money would convert district sites that are no longer in use into below-market rental housing for teachers and staff. It mentions redeveloping a closed school site or other district property as a possibility. We have not seen a specific site, number of units or timeline confirmed in district materials. Neighbors of district-owned property may want to follow board agendas for details.

How it fits with earlier bonds

San Mateo-Foster City voters passed Measure X ($148 million) in 2015 and Measure T ($409 million) in 2020. The Daily Journal reported in May 2026 that Measure X was effectively all spent and about 75% of Measure T had been spent. The district also says it may qualify for about $53 million in additional state matching funds. When the district surveyed voters in August 2025, about 57% said they would support a $498 million measure, according to the Daily Journal.

What it could cost you

The tax is based on your assessed value on the county tax roll, not your home's market value. Under Proposition 13, assessed value generally starts at your purchase price and can rise by no more than 2% a year. At the district's estimated $29 per $100,000:

  • A $600,000 assessed value would pay about $174 a year
  • A $1.2 million assessed value would pay about $348 a year
  • A $2 million assessed value would pay about $580 a year

The district notes that state law doesn't allow senior exemptions on these bonds. It also says renters would not pay the tax.

A second bond on the same ballot: Measure V

Voters across San Mateo County will also decide Measure V, an $848 million bond for the San Mateo County Community College District. That district runs College of San Mateo, Cañada College and Skyline College in San Bruno. According to the Palo Alto Daily Post, Measure V would extend an existing levy of about $18 per $100,000 of assessed value rather than add a new one. The levy would last until about 2049. The Almanac reported a lower estimate of $10.50 per $100,000 that could rise to $18. Check the official voter guide for the final figures. Measure V also needs 55% to pass.

What homeowners, buyers and sellers may want to do

  • Homeowners: Find your assessed value on your current property tax bill and multiply to estimate the cost. Voter-approved bond taxes appear as separate line items on your county tax bill.
  • Buyers: Your assessed value will generally reset to your purchase price. Budget for these line items when you estimate your monthly payment, and ask your lender to use realistic tax figures.
  • Sellers: Buyers often ask about the tax bill, so it helps to have your current bill handy.
  • Small landlords: If you have questions about passing costs through to tenants or about deductions, talk to a tax professional or attorney.

Your official county voter guide will include the full text of both measures, an impartial analysis, and the arguments for and against.

Sources

  • San Mateo-Foster City School District: Workforce Housing
  • Local News Matters: San Mateo November 3, 2026
  • Patch: San Mateo Voter Guide 2026

  • San Mateo Daily Journal: Bowditch Middle School unveils new gym, classrooms and library

title: San Jose Council Upholds Data Center Permit for Nvidia-Leased North San Jose Building
summary: San Jose's City Council rejected an appeal and kept a data center permit in place for an Nvidia-leased building at 300 Holger Way. Here's what changes.
html:
The San Jose City Council has turned down an appeal and kept in place a city permit that lets a North San Jose research building operate as a data center. Nvidia leases the building at 300 Holger Way. With the vote, the city has finished its review of the permit. The decision also comes as San Jose works on citywide rules for data centers, and residents can weigh in on those rules at public hearings in November and December.

What the council decided

San José Spotlight reports that the council voted unanimously on Tuesday, October 20, to reject the appeal. Councilmember Peter Ortiz was absent, and Vice Mayor Pam Foley recused herself because of a financial conflict of interest. San Jose Inside, carrying a CalMatters report, gives the count as 8–0. The Real Deal, citing the Mercury News, says three councilmembers did not vote and that Foley said she has a financial interest in the tenant.

The appeal targeted a decision city planners made on July 8. That decision approved a Special Use Permit to run a data center using up to 20 megawatts of power inside the existing research and development building. According to the City of San José's planning website, data centers in the city need a Special Use Permit, which is heard at a Planning Director's Hearing.

The site: size, location and scope

  • Location: 300 Holger Way in North San Jose, just south of Highway 237, in Council District 4. Councilmember David Cohen represents the district (San José Spotlight).
  • Size: A building of about 97,800 square feet on a 4.86-acre property, according to Data Center Dynamics, which reviewed the planning documents.
  • Owner and tenant: Real estate investment firm Menlo Equities owns the building. Nvidia began leasing it in December 2024, and the lease runs through 2035 (Data Center Dynamics, The Real Deal).
  • What the permit allows: Only work inside the building, including installing data racks. Planning documents say the project would not change the outside of the building or add to its footprint (San José Spotlight, Data Center Dynamics).

We could not confirm a current construction schedule. Planning documents described in Mercury News coverage, republished by Industry Insider in December 2025, said data center work would begin in December 2026 and finish by July 2027. Since then, the owner has described the permit mainly as covering research work that is already happening in the building, so that earlier schedule may no longer apply.

Why the permit was appealed

The appeal came from Citizens for Responsible Industry, a labor-backed group, along with residents who share its concerns. They argued that the project should have gone through a full environmental review. They also said the facility's possible noise and air pollution could affect people living nearby. The group's attorney, Kelilah Federman, told the council that a 20-megawatt facility would need major electrical and cooling upgrades that the city did not consider (San José Spotlight).

City planners answered that no further review was needed because the permit covers only interior changes and allows no new construction. City officials also said the owner would need a separate permit before adding new equipment to the site.

What the owner says the building is used for

Erik Schoennauer, a land use consultant for Menlo Equities, told San José Spotlight that Nvidia has run a chip-testing lab in the building for years. He said the lab includes a data hall supplied with 8.5 megawatts of power, and that Nvidia plans to keep running it. Menlo Equities says it applied because the city defines "data center" very broadly, and the testing work could fall under that definition. Menlo Equities partner Jane Vaughan said Nvidia has spent about $100 million remodeling the building for testing and research (San José Spotlight, The Real Deal).

Councilmember Cohen agreed that the city's definition needs updating. He said the building is not a data center in the usual sense and that the city code's definition is "very strange." The city's planning website now separates the two: data centers mainly rent server space to other companies, while "large energy-use projects" use a lot of power for a company's own work.

Citywide data center rules: key dates

San Jose Inside reports that the council has decided against a temporary moratorium on data centers. Instead, the city is writing permanent standards for data centers and large energy-use projects of 20 megawatts or more. The draft schedule:

  • November 18: Planning Commission review
  • December 8: City Council hearing and planned vote

The deadline for public comments to appear in the official staff reports was October 22. Residents can still send letters and speak at either hearing. Meanwhile, Oakland, San Francisco and Gilroy have recently adopted temporary moratoriums on new data centers.

What this means for homeowners, buyers and sellers

For people living near Holger Way, the permit allows no outside construction or building expansion. City officials say any new equipment would need its own permit. Several other data center applications are pending in North San Jose. The city's list includes 2549 Orchard Parkway and 350 W. Trimble Road, both still under environmental review.

  • Follow the hearings. The November and December meetings will set rules on issues like water use, energy use and community benefits.
  • Look up nearby projects. The city's planning website lists data center applications. You can find details for each one by file number at SJPermits.org.
  • Buying near North San Jose's industrial areas? During your contingency period, check the permit history and pending applications nearby. If you have questions about a specific property, an attorney can help.

We'll keep watching how San Jose's data center rules develop and what they mean for homes in North San Jose and the rest of the city.

Sources

  • The Real Deal: Nvidia gets final city approval for data center in north San Jose (Oct. 23, 2026)
  • San José Spotlight: San Jose data center advances after pushback (Oct. 22, 2026)
  • San Jose Inside / CalMatters: San Jose, Santa Clara Avoid Moves Taken by Other CA Cities to Pull Plug on New Data Centers (Oct. 22, 2026)
  • Data Center Dynamics: Plan for data center at Nvidia site in San Jose faces appeal (July 23, 2026)
  • Industry Insider California (Mercury News via TNS): Nvidia-Leased San Jose Building Poised to Become Major AI Data Center (Dec. 2, 2025)

title: San Mateo-Foster City Schools' $498M Measure W: What Property Owners Should Know
summary: Measure W on the Nov. 3 ballot would fund classroom upgrades and about 80 staff homes in San Mateo, at an estimated $29 per $100,000 of assessed value.
html:
If you own a home or a rental property in San Mateo or Foster City, you'll see a school bond on your November ballot. Measure W would let the San Mateo-Foster City School District issue up to $498 million in bonds to pay for campus upgrades and housing for teachers and staff. The district runs the TK–8 public schools in both cities. Below we cover what the measure would pay for, what it could add to your property tax bill and the key dates.

The basics: what's on the ballot and when

The district says its Board of Trustees adopted Resolution No. 06/25-26, which places the bond on the November 3, 2026 statewide general election ballot. The San Mateo County Elections Office lists it as "Measure W – San Mateo-Foster City School District: Bond Measure." It needs 55% of the votes cast on it to pass. The county's election page also links to the measure's full text, the tax rate statement, an impartial analysis and the arguments for and against. We suggest reading those before you vote.

What it would cost property owners

The district estimates the bond would cost property owners $29 per $100,000 of assessed value each year. The tax is based on the assessed value on your county tax bill, not on what your home would sell for today. A home with an assessed value of $1,000,000, for example, would pay about $290 a year. San Mateo County's elections office also lists other measures on the same ballot. One is Measure V, a separate bond for the San Mateo County Community College District.

Some points from the district's FAQ:

  • State law doesn't allow a senior exemption on school bonds of this kind, so the tax applies to all taxable property in the district.
  • Under Proposition 13, assessed values usually rise no more than 2% a year. That means longtime owners usually pay less than recent buyers.
  • The district says renters are exempt because the tax is charged to property owners.

Hoodline summarized reporting from the San Mateo Daily Journal on how this bond would stack with the district's existing ones. The bonds would be repaid over 30 years. Owners already pay Measure T, a $409 million bond approved in 2020, at about $30 per $100,000 through 2051. They also pay Measure X, a $148 million bond from 2015, at about $14.80 per $100,000, which is set to end by 2044. If Measure W passes, the three bonds together would come to about $73.80 per $100,000 of assessed value. Actual rates can change from year to year, so check your own tax bill for the exact figure.

The district also collects a separate parcel tax, Measure V from 2019, which is not the same as the college bond above. The Daily Journal reported in 2025 that this parcel tax is $349.40 per parcel a year and runs through 2028. It also reported that the district expects to seek a renewal.

Where the money would go

The district's bond page lists these estimated priority costs:

  • Workforce housing: $100 million
  • Replacing windowless classrooms: $84 million
  • Science, music and career technical education spaces: $69 million
  • Bowditch Middle School campus rebuild: $59 million
  • Classroom and site modernizations: $49 million
  • Furniture: $38 million
  • Painting: $31 million

Specific campus projects on the district's list include:

  • Science, music and career-education space at Abbott Middle School
  • Replacing classroom "pods" at Audubon Elementary and San Mateo Park Elementary
  • New science, music and library buildings at Bayside Academy and Borel Middle School

The list also covers fire alarms, roofing, window replacement and classroom technology. The district says many of its classrooms were built about 70 years ago. It also says many campuses have leaky roofs and fire alarms that are 25 years old. According to the Daily Journal, as reported by Hoodline, the district has identified more than $1 billion in total facility needs, with about $524 million considered urgent over the next five to 10 years.

Proposed staff housing at the Knolls Campus

For homeowners near 42nd Avenue in San Mateo, the housing plan may be the part to watch most closely. The district's workforce housing page says its Workforce Housing Leadership Subcommittee looked at two district-owned sites. One was the Knolls Campus at 525 42nd Ave., a former elementary school site. The other was the district office property on Chess Drive in Foster City. Early feasibility studies found room for about 80 units at either site. In February 2026, the subcommittee recommended pursuing housing only at the Knolls Campus.

This project is still at the concept stage. We found no approved site plan, building height or unit design yet. As reported by Hoodline, the Daily Journal says the housing would be among the first projects if Measure W passes. Using a design-build approach, district officials estimate it could be finished within about four years. The district says 608 employees answered its staff housing survey, and 96% said housing costs make it hard to recruit and keep staff.

The debate

Support for the bond isn't guaranteed. The Daily Journal reported that a 2025 district survey found about 57% of likely voters in favor, just above the 55% needed. Consultants said that was lower than in past polling. According to the Daily Journal's reporting as summarized by Hoodline, at least one resident has criticized the cost and the ongoing operating expenses. That resident suggested the district work with a private or nonprofit developer on the housing instead of owning it outright. The district points to its required safeguards: an independent citizens' oversight committee, annual audits, and a rule that no bond money can go to administrators' salaries or pensions.

What this means for homeowners, buyers and sellers

  • Homeowners: Find the assessed value on your San Mateo County tax bill and multiply by the estimated rate to see what the bond might cost you. Then read the county's voter materials before November 3.
  • Buyers: After a purchase, the assessed value resets to roughly the price you paid, so bond charges are based on that number. Ask your lender to include voter-approved taxes in your payment estimate, and check the "special assessments" and "voter-approved debt" lines on the seller's most recent tax bill.
  • Sellers: If Measure W passes, buyers and their agents will likely ask about the new charge, so it helps to have your current tax bill ready.
  • Small landlords: The tax is charged to owners. If you have questions about how it affects your rental's finances, talk with a tax professional.
